theme/science.title: Science
theme/science.summary: Science is the systematic study of the natural world through observation, measurement, mathematics, and testing, together with the habits and institutions that let people check and extend one another's claims. Its practices run from the counting, calendar-keeping, and sky-watching of prehistoric peoples, through the mathematics, astronomy, and medicine of the early literate states and the scholarly centers of the medieval world, to the experimental sciences of Europe from the sixteenth century and the genomics, computing, and Earth-system research of the twenty-first. Traditions of careful observation arose independently in many regions, and modern science grew from several of them rather than from one. This hub gathers the vault's notes on scientists, institutions, instruments, and discoveries, and on the events that changed how knowledge of nature was made and passed on.
theme/science.observer: The Observer calls this pattern-taming: the species' long effort to find regularities in nature, record them, and use them to predict. Counting, calendars, and careful observation appear in many places long before the modern period, so what looks distinctive about the modern form is its institutionalized doubt, in which strangers agree to check one another's claims and to publish what they find. That habit rests on memory-outsourcing (writing, paper, printing) and on exchange-webs that carried instruments, texts, and people, and it works against ancestor-weight, since the older authority is often the first claim to be tested. This reading would weaken if institutionalized doubt proves to have been as old and as widespread as counting itself, or if it turns out to depend on something other than writing and travel.
questions: How did the culture of open criticism emerge and spread, and where did it exist in institutions before the seventeenth century?
How much of the Scientific Revolution rested on knowledge that moved from the Islamic world, India, and China, and how can that debt be measured?
What can be recovered of scientific traditions that were carried by oral teaching, songlines, and cord records?
Why did centers of learning such as the Library of Alexandria, Baghdad, and Samarkand decline, and what was lost when they did?
Why do major discoveries so often arise independently in more than one mind or place, as with the calculus and natural selection?

extra.title: Key Threads
extra.html:
• Counting, calendars, and sky-watching are among the oldest organized knowledge. The axis of Stonehenge aligns with the solstice sunrise and sunset, buildings and rock carvings at Chaco Canyon align with the sun and moon, and the Maya kept precise calendars.
  • Writing turned observation into records that others could check. Invention of Writing began in Mesopotamia as accounting, and Mesopotamian scribes, from the time of the Sumerians, worked in a base-60 number system that survives in the division of the hour and the circle.
  • The Ancient Egyptians left medical papyri, such as the Edwin Smith papyrus of about 1600 BCE, that set out the examination and treatment of injuries case by case; see Nile Valley.
  • The Axial Age brought new traditions of reasoned inquiry in Greece, India, and China; see Confucius and the Ancient Greeks.
  • Greek natural philosophy sought general causes. Aristotle studied physics and biology, including careful observation of marine life; the Library of Alexandria supported scholars such as Eratosthenes, who estimated the circumference of the Earth; and Hypatia taught mathematics and astronomy in Alexandria. See also Athens.
  • The decimal place-value system with zero developed in India in the first millennium CE and spread west; see Zero and Place-Value Notation and the Gupta Empire. The age of the earliest zero, in the Bakhshali manuscript, is contested.
  • Under the Abbasid Caliphate, the Translation Movement and the House of Wisdom rendered Greek, Persian, Syriac, and Indian works into Arabic and extended them. The arithmetic and algebra of Al-Khwarizmi gave later languages the words algorithm and algebra, and Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine was used in European universities into the 17th century. Al-Andalus became another center of learning.
  • Observatories, libraries, and manuscript collections grew along the Silk Roads and the Saharan routes. Ulugh Beg's observatory at Samarkand produced a star catalogue of at least 1,018 stars, and Timbuktu holds hundreds of thousands of historical manuscripts.
  • Pacific navigators crossed thousands of kilometers using star paths, swells, and bird flight rather than instruments; see Polynesian Settlement of the Pacific and Polynesians.
  • Instruments extended what could be measured and shared: the Magnetic Compass in China by about the 12th century, the Mechanical Clock (Su Song's astronomical clock tower of 1088; weight-driven clocks in European towns about 1300), and the Movable-Type Printing Press of about 1440.
  • The Scientific Revolution (roughly 1543 to 1687) made experiment, mathematics, and observation central; see Galileo Galilei and Isaac Newton. It drew on earlier work in the Islamic world, India, and China.
  • The Enlightenment carried a preference for evidence into public life. In 1796 Edward Jenner showed that cowpox inoculation protected against smallpox, the start of Vaccination; smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980.
  • The 19th and early 20th centuries brought evolution by natural selection (Charles Darwin), radioactivity (Marie Curie), relativity (Albert Einstein), and what is often regarded as the first published computer algorithm (Ada Lovelace); the Meiji Restoration and the Tanzimat Reforms were state programs to acquire the new sciences and their institutions.
  • Late 20th-century science gave computation (Alan Turing, Digital Computer), the structure of DNA (Rosalind Franklin, Genomic Revolution), and spaceflight (Space Age, Moon Landing); Rachel Carson, Modern Climate Change, the Jack Hills Zircons, and the Tunguska Event show Earth-system science at work.

extra.title: Through the Eras
extra.html:
• Paleolithic: Working knowledge of stone, fire, animals, and plants accumulates (Oldowan Stone Tools, Control of Fire, Emergence of Symbolic Art). Aboriginal Australians managed the landscape with fire and passed on ecological knowledge through oral traditions and songlines. Notched bones from this era may be tallies, though their purpose is debated.
  • Neolithic: Farmers select seed and stock over generations (Domestication of Maize, Domestication of Rice, Animal Domestication), and builders align monuments with the sun (Stonehenge).
  • Bronze Age: Writing lets scribes keep records, tables, and observations (Invention of Writing, Sumerians, Ancient Egyptians); Mesopotamian arithmetic uses base 60, and Egyptian medical texts describe cases and treatments.
  • Iron Age: Reasoned inquiry into nature and human affairs appears in the Axial Age in Greece, India, and China (Confucius, Ancient Greeks); Polynesian voyagers build up knowledge of stars and swells (Polynesians).
  • Classical Antiquity: Athens and Aristotle, the Library of Alexandria and Hypatia, and in India Zero and Place-Value Notation under the Gupta Empire. The Han Dynasty kept astronomical records, and its scholar Zhang Heng built a seismoscope in 132 CE. The Opening of the Silk Roads moved ideas along with goods.
  • Medieval Period: The Translation Movement and the House of Wisdom, Al-Khwarizmi, Ibn Sina, and Al-Andalus; the Song Dynasty's Magnetic Compass and Gunpowder; the Maya calendar and astronomy; Chaco Canyon; Ulugh Beg and the Timurid Empire; Timbuktu; Ibn Khaldun's theory of how states rise and fall; the Mechanical Clock; the Renaissance.
  • Early Modern Period: The Scientific Revolution (Galileo Galilei, Isaac Newton), the Enlightenment, and Vaccination (1796).
  • Industrial Age: The Industrial Revolution created new demand for measurement and engineering. Charles Darwin, Ada Lovelace, Marie Curie, Albert Einstein, Antibiotics, Nuclear Fission, and the Electrical Power Grid belong here, as do state modernization programs such as the Meiji Restoration and Tanzimat Reforms.
  • Information Age: Alan Turing and the Digital Computer, Rosalind Franklin and the Genomic Revolution, the Space Age and Moon Landing, Rachel Carson and Modern Climate Change, the Green Revolution, and the COVID-19 Pandemic, in which mRNA vaccines were developed and authorized within about a year.

extra.title: Regional Patterns
extra.html:
• Mesopotamia and the Nile Valley: The earliest written mathematics, astronomy, and medicine are tied to temple and palace administration; see Sumerians and Ancient Egyptians.
  • South Asia and the Islamic world: Place-value notation with zero arose in India and was carried west by scholars of the Abbasid Caliphate and Al-Andalus; Latin translations of Arabic texts fed European scholarship in the 12th century.
  • East Asia: Paper, printing, the compass, and gunpowder were documented first in China, and the Song Dynasty was a center of technical and commercial innovation.
  • Central Asia: The oases were a crossroads for learning. Ibn Sina was born near Bukhara, Ulugh Beg built his observatory at Samarkand, and the Timurid Empire patronized it; see Central Asian Oases.
  • Oceania: Polynesian voyagers navigated without instruments (Polynesians), the Kuk Early Agricultural Site preserves at least 7,000 years of wetland gardening, and the Jack Hills Zircons in Western Australia hold the oldest known pieces of Earth's crust, about 4.4 billion years old.
  • Mesoamerica and the Andes: The Maya kept precise calendars and used the concept of zero, and the Andean Quipu recorded numbers in a decimal system on knotted cords.
  • Sub-Saharan Africa: Scholarship in Timbuktu and much of the fossil evidence for human origins (Divergence of the Hominin Lineage, Origin of Homo sapiens) come from this region.
  • Siberia and the Arctic: The Tunguska Event of 1908 was first studied on site by an expedition in 1927, and Arctic peoples such as the Inuit built up detailed knowledge of ice, weather, and animal behavior for survival (Inuit and the Thule Expansion).

extra.title: Debates and Limits
extra.html:
• Whether star-lore, navigation, and Indigenous ecological knowledge should be called science, or only the experimental and mathematical tradition of recent centuries, is disputed. This hub uses a broad definition and treats the narrower one as a later development.
  • Historians debate whether the Scientific Revolution was a single revolution and how much it owed to earlier work in the Islamic world, India, and China. The exact nature of the House of Wisdom is also debated, and the Library of Alexandria declined over centuries rather than in one fire.
  • Credit is contested in many cases: the earliest zero (Zero and Place-Value Notation), the calculus, which Isaac Newton developed independently of Leibniz, natural selection, which Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace reached separately, the use of Rosalind Franklin's X-ray data in the double-helix model, and Lise Meitner's exclusion from the 1944 Nobel Prize for Nuclear Fission.
  • Science that was carried by oral teaching, songlines, and cord records left few written texts, so it is easy to undercount.
  • The vault's science notes lean toward Europe, the Islamic world, and named individuals. It has few notes on scientists in Africa south of the Sahara, Oceania, the Andes, and Mesoamerica, and none yet on Indian astronomy or Chinese mathematics as topics in their own right.

theme/technology.title: Technology
theme/technology.summary: Technology is the making and use of tools, techniques, and systems to extend what people can do. It is cumulative: each generation builds on the tools of the last, and the record runs from the first chipped stones, at least 2.6 million years ago, through fire, pottery, farming, metals, writing, and printing, to engines, electric grids, and digital networks. This hub covers materials, energy, transport, information, food, medicine, and the built environment, and it links the vault's technology notes to the events, places, and peoples through which techniques arose and spread. Many techniques arose independently in more than one region, and others crossed continents within a few centuries.
theme/technology.observer: The Observer calls this the tool-lineage: an inheritance in which each tool makes the next possible. The lineage branches rather than running in a single line, and it sometimes breaks when a technique dies with its makers, yet similar solutions such as farming and writing appear in unconnected branches, which suggests that some steps are shaped by shared needs and materials as well as by chance. Memory-outsourcing made the lineage far easier to carry across generations, and ancestor-weight can keep a working technique in use long after alternatives exist. The lineage is now old enough that no single person understands the whole of it. The Observer would revise this reading if apparent independent origins prove to be diffusion after all, or if the loss of techniques turns out to be much more common than the record shows.
questions: Do technologies follow a predictable order, or are they contingent?
Why did some techniques arise independently in several regions, such as farming and writing, while others, such as wheeled transport, were not used in the Americas before contact?
How much perishable technology (wood, cord, cloth, basketry) is missing from the record, and how can its scale be estimated?
Where did the pace of change shift decisively: with fire, farming, writing, the steam engine, or the Great Acceleration?
How were techniques carried between cultures, by traders, craftspeople, captives, missionaries, and armies, and which traditional stories, such as papermaking at Battle of Talas, survive scrutiny?

extra.title: Key Threads
extra.html:
• Stone tools begin at least 2.6 million years ago in Africa; see Oldowan Stone Tools and Homo habilis, and, later, the handaxes made by Homo erectus.
  • Control of Fire is an early energy technology. Evidence at Wonderwerk Cave in South Africa dates to about one million years ago, habitual use is well established by about 400,000 years ago, and cooked food may have supported larger brains.
  • Pottery appears in East Asia at least 20,000 years ago, well before farming; see Jomon Culture.
  • Farming and herding arose independently in several regions and brought new techniques: see The Agricultural Revolution, Animal Domestication, Domestication of Rice in the Yangtze region, Domestication of Maize in Mexico, and the drained wetland gardens of the Kuk Early Agricultural Site in New Guinea.
  • Wheeled vehicles appear around 3500 to 3000 BCE (The Wheel). Bronze, an alloy of copper and tin, was first widely produced in the Near East around 3300 BCE, and tin had to be traded over long distances (Bronze Metallurgy). On the steppe, the Botai Culture managed horses and the Sintashta Culture built the earliest known spoke-wheeled chariots.
  • Recording systems arose in several places. Invention of Writing happened independently at least three or four times, first in Mesopotamia about 3400 to 3200 BCE; the Alphabet (Proto-Sinaitic, about 1800 BCE) gave rise to most alphabets in use today; and in the Andes knotted cords served as records (Quipu, with possible early relatives at Caral).
  • Iron smelting began on a limited scale in Anatolia in the early 2nd millennium BCE and spread widely from about 1200 BCE (Iron Smelting). Ironworking in Africa, including at Meroe in the Kingdom of Kush and among Bantu-speaking peoples (Bantu Expansion), is a case where independent invention is debated.
  • Paper was developed in China between about the 2nd century BCE and the 2nd century CE (Paper, Han Dynasty). Woodblock Printing produced the Diamond Sutra of 868, the oldest dated printed book, and movable type appeared in China about 1040 and in Korea (metal type) in 1377 before Johannes Gutenberg's Movable-Type Printing Press in Mainz about 1440.
  • Under the Song Dynasty gunpowder became a military technology and the compass was used for navigation at sea; see Gunpowder and Magnetic Compass. Su Song built an astronomical clock tower in 1088, and weight-driven mechanical clocks with escapements appeared in European towns about 1300 (Mechanical Clock).
  • Ocean and polar travel: Polynesians settled the remote Pacific in double-hulled canoes using non-instrument navigation (Polynesian Settlement of the Pacific); the Thule ancestors of the Inuit used dog sleds, skin boats, and toggling harpoons (Inuit and the Thule Expansion); and the Norse crossed the North Atlantic, reaching L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland by 1021.
  • Large-scale landscape engineering appears in many regions: the reservoirs and canals of Angkor and the Khmer Empire, the earthworks and enriched soils of Amazonian Urbanism and Dark Earths (see Upano Valley Settlements and Xingu Garden Cities), the road system of the Inca Empire, roughly 30,000 to 40,000 kilometers long, and the dry-stone walls of Great Zimbabwe.
  • Steam power (Steam Engine: Newcomen 1712, Watt's separate condenser patented 1769) drove the Industrial Revolution and made Railways possible; the Telegraph and Submarine Cables then carried messages across oceans, and works such as the Suez Canal (1869) and the Trans-Siberian Railway (1891 to 1916) followed.
  • The Electrical Power Grid began with the first commercial power station in 1882. Nuclear Fission, discovered in 1938, led to reactors and weapons (Nuclear Age). Vaccination (1796), Antibiotics (1928), and the Green Revolution changed health and food supply.
  • The Digital Computer (ENIAC, 1945) shrank with the transistor (1947) and the integrated circuit (about 1958). The Digital Revolution brought the internet (1969), the World Wide Web (1991), and smartphones (about 2007), and the Space Age began with Sputnik in 1957; see Alan Turing.

extra.title: Through the Eras
extra.html:
• Paleolithic: Oldowan Stone Tools, Control of Fire, the handaxes of Homo erectus, Pottery about 20,000 years ago, open-sea crossings to Sahul at least 50,000 years ago (Peopling of Sahul), and the wooden hut foundations, leather, and rope preserved at Monte Verde.
  • Neolithic: Farming and herding (The Agricultural Revolution, Animal Domestication, Domestication of Rice, Domestication of Maize), stone building at Jericho, where a wall and tower date to roughly 8000 BCE, pottery-making hunter-gatherers (Jomon Culture), and artificial mummification from about 5050 BCE (Chinchorro Culture).
  • Bronze Age: The Wheel, Bronze Metallurgy, Invention of Writing, the Alphabet, and cities (The Urban Revolution); planned streets, drainage, and standard weights in the Indus Valley Civilization; spoke-wheeled chariots (Sintashta Culture); large stone construction at Giza Necropolis and platform mounds at Caral.
  • Iron Age: Iron Smelting, ironworking at Meroe in the Kingdom of Kush, farming and ironworking carried by the Bantu Expansion, and Pacific voyaging by the Polynesians.
  • Classical Antiquity: Paper under the Han Dynasty; the standardization of writing, weights, measures, and currency in the Unification of China under Qin; roads, aqueducts, and concrete in the Romans' empire; Zero and Place-Value Notation in India; and, from about 500 BCE, the settlement networks of Amazonian Urbanism and Dark Earths and the Upano Valley Settlements.
  • Medieval Period: Woodblock Printing, Gunpowder, the Magnetic Compass, the Mechanical Clock, the Quipu, and the Movable-Type Printing Press; water works at Angkor; stone building at Great Zimbabwe; Norse and Thule seafaring (Norse, Inuit and the Thule Expansion); and the Inca royal estate at Machu Picchu.
  • Early Modern Period: The first commercially successful Steam Engine (1712); ocean routes opened by ships armed with cannon (Portuguese Sea Route to India); crops and animals crossing the Atlantic (Columbian Exchange); instruments and print in the Scientific Revolution; and Vaccination in 1796.
  • Industrial Age: The Industrial Revolution, Railways (1825), the Telegraph and Submarine Cables (1844), the Electrical Power Grid (1882), the Trans-Siberian Railway, the Suez Canal, Antibiotics (1928), and Nuclear Fission (1938). States such as Egypt under Muhammad Ali of Egypt, Japan in the Meiji Restoration, and Ethiopia under Menelik II sought to acquire industrial and military technology.
  • Information Age: The Digital Computer, the Digital Revolution, the Nuclear Age, the Green Revolution, the Space Age and Moon Landing, the Genomic Revolution (CRISPR gene editing, 2012), and the Great Acceleration, in which energy and fertilizer use have risen steeply since about 1950.

extra.title: Regional Patterns
extra.html:
• East Asia: Pottery, paper, printing, gunpowder, and the compass were documented first here. Several reached the west along the Silk Roads and through the Mongol Empire; see Opening of the Silk Roads.
  • Sub-Saharan Africa: The earliest known stone tools come from here (Oldowan Stone Tools), as does much of the debate over African ironworking; the Bantu Expansion carried farming and iron across the continent, and Great Zimbabwe shows dry-stone building at scale.
  • Andes: The Quipu recorded numbers on knotted cords, the Chinchorro Culture practiced the earliest known deliberate artificial mummification, and the Inca Empire built a road system of tens of thousands of kilometers. The wheel was not used for transport in the Americas before contact (The Wheel).
  • Mesoamerica: Maize was domesticated here, and cooking it with lime (nixtamalization) makes its nutrients available (Domestication of Maize). Tenochtitlan was fed in part by chinampas, and the Maya developed a full writing system.
  • Oceania: People crossed open sea to Sahul at least 50,000 years ago (Peopling of Sahul), cultivated drained wetlands in New Guinea (Kuk Early Agricultural Site), and later settled the far Pacific (Polynesians).
  • Central Asian Steppe: Horse management at Botai Culture sites and spoke-wheeled chariots at Sintashta Culture settlements come from the steppe.
  • Siberia and the Arctic: Inuit and the Thule Expansion shows cold-climate technology (dog sleds, skin boats, toggling harpoons), Yakut (Sakha) herders adapted horses and cattle to one of the coldest inhabited regions, and the Trans-Siberian Railway later crossed the region.
  • Southeast Asia and the Amazon Basin and South American Lowlands: Both regions show large-scale water and soil engineering, from the reservoirs of Angkor to the dark earths and earthworks of Amazonian Urbanism and Dark Earths.

extra.title: Debates and Limits
extra.html:
• Independent invention versus diffusion is disputed in many cases. Writing arose independently at least three or four times, but scholars are divided on whether African ironworking was independent of the Near East, and the spread of papermaking and printing across Eurasia is traced only in part.
  • Single-inventor stories usually compress long processes. Movable type was used in China and Korea before Gutenberg, paper fragments predate the traditional date credited to Cai Lun, and the Steam Engine of Newcomen preceded Watt's improvements.
  • The record is biased toward durable materials. Wood, cord, cloth, and basketry rarely survive, Spanish colonial authorities banned or destroyed many quipus (Quipu), and earlier stone tools than the Oldowan, such as reports from Lomekwi in Kenya of about 3.3 million years ago, remain under study.
  • Whether technologies drive social change or are shaped by it is contested, and this hub does not settle it.
  • The vault's coverage is uneven. It has no notes yet on optics, sanitation, aviation, semiconductors, or GPS as technologies, and few on non-Western techniques such as crucible steel, porcelain, qanats, chinampas, or outrigger canoes.

theme/trade-and-economy.title: Trade and Economy
theme/trade-and-economy.summary: Trade and economy cover the production, exchange, and taxation of goods, labor, and money, and the institutions that organize them: markets, credit, coinage, companies, tribute, and forced labor. The vault traces exchange from the long-distance movement of stone and shells in prehistory, through Bronze Age metal trade, the Silk Road, Indian Ocean, and trans-Saharan networks, and the global commerce created after 1492, to the industrial production and digital economy of the twentieth and twenty-first centuries. Trade moved ideas, religions, crops, and diseases along with goods, and it also included the coerced trade in people. This hub gathers the vault's notes on routes, trading states, commodities, and economic systems.
theme/trade-and-economy.observer: The Observer calls these exchange-webs and notes that they have no owner or center. Trade repeatedly makes strangers into partners, and transmits pathogens as readily as products. The record suggests that exchange-webs rest on trust that has to be built through shared accounts, coinage, law, and other story-glue, and that they sit beside coercive extraction, such as tribute, forced labor, and the trade in people, which the Observer records in the same ledger rather than in a separate one (see Frontiers of Extraction). Networks that carried goods also carried ideas, religions, crops, and diseases, so the Observer does not treat them as merely economic. This reading would weaken if long-distance trade proves to have been driven mainly by states and elites, with little of the decentralized quality the term implies.
questions: How did early markets and money emerge?
How much long-distance exchange before writing can be reconstructed from materials alone, and how reliable are the inferences?
Why did some exchange routes last for centuries, such as the Silk Roads, the Indian Ocean, and the trans-Saharan routes, while others collapsed, as in the Bronze Age Collapse?
How did trade, tribute, and coercion interact in empires such as the Aztec Empire, the Inca Empire, the Romans, and the Qing Dynasty?
Why did sustained growth in output per person begin when and where it did?
How far did trade spread disease, from the Black Death to the 1918 Influenza Pandemic and the COVID-19 Pandemic, and how did societies respond?

extra.title: Key Threads
extra.html:
• Long-distance exchange of stone and shells goes back tens of thousands of years. The Lapita Culture moved obsidian and other goods over long distances across the western Pacific, and the hunter-gatherer-fishers of Poverty Point in Louisiana brought in stone and other materials from hundreds of kilometers away between about 1700 and 1100 BCE.
  • Farming supported denser populations and permanent settlement (The Agricultural Revolution), and the first cities followed (The Urban Revolution, Uruk, Sumerians). Invention of Writing began as a way to record goods and obligations, and the earliest tablets from Uruk are accounting records. Bronze Metallurgy made trade essential because tin was scarce and had to be carried over long distances from places such as Afghanistan and later Cornwall.
  • Bronze Age networks tied the eastern Mediterranean, Anatolia, Egypt, and the Indus. The Indus Valley Civilization traded with Mesopotamia and made goods to standard weights, the Minoans traded across the eastern Mediterranean, and Hatshepsut sponsored a trading expedition to Punt. The Bronze Age Collapse around 1200 BCE ended the palace economies, and the breakdown of trade networks is among the proposed causes.
  • Caravan and sea traders grew rich as middlemen. The Incense Trade carried frankincense and myrrh from southern Arabia and the Horn of Africa by camel caravan; the Kingdom of Saba and the Nabataeans profited from taxing and guiding the caravans; and the Phoenicians of the Levant coast founded colonies, including Carthage, and spread a simple alphabet.
  • The Opening of the Silk Roads from the second century BCE linked East Asia, South Asia, Central Asia, and the Mediterranean. Goods included silk, horses, glass, spices, and paper, and disease also traveled the routes (Black Death). The Han Dynasty paid the Xiongnu annual gifts, the Kushan Empire connected Rome, Parthia, India, and Han China commercially, and the Sogdians became the leading Silk Road merchants, acting as caravan leaders, interpreters, and bankers.
  • Large states built economies around roads, taxation, and records. The Romans were tied together by Latin, Greek, and trade, Augustus reorganized the army, provinces, and taxation, the Kingdom of Aksum controlled Red Sea trade between Rome, Arabia, and India and minted its own coins, and the Persepolis tablets of the Achaemenid Persians record rations and administration (Persepolis).
  • The Indian Ocean Trade Network used the monsoon winds and was busiest from about the 8th to the 15th century, carrying spices, cotton textiles, ivory, gold, and Chinese porcelain. The Swahili Coast City-States, such as Kilwa, which minted its own coins, grew rich from it; Srivijaya controlled shipping through the Strait of Malacca; the Chola Dynasty traded with China and Southeast Asia; and the Malacca Sultanate became the leading port of Southeast Asia in the 15th century before the Portuguese took it in 1511 (Portuguese Sea Route to India).
  • Trans-Saharan trade in gold, salt, and ivory sustained the Ghana Empire, the Mali Empire, and the Songhai Empire. Mansa Musa's pilgrimage in 1324 reportedly disrupted the gold market in Cairo, and Timbuktu became a hub of trade and scholarship. Farther south, Great Zimbabwe traded gold and ivory with the Swahili coast, and the Kingdom of Mapungubwe received glass beads and Chinese celadon through East African harbors.
  • East Asia was a commercial center. The Tang Dynasty's capital Chang'an held about a million people; the Song Dynasty issued some of the world's first government paper money; American silver, arriving through the Manila trade, became a major part of the Ming Dynasty economy; and the Tokugawa Shogunate limited foreign trade to Dutch and Chinese merchants at Nagasaki.
  • Exchange and tribute in the pre-Columbian Americas took forms unlike those of Eurasia. Caral combined coastal fishing with inland farming, Teotihuacan had wide trade and political links, Chaco Canyon was a ceremonial and trade center with roads radiating from it, the Aztec Empire collected tribute from conquered city-states, and the Inca Empire exacted labor service (mit'a) rather than money taxes and kept records on Quipu.
  • After 1492 trade became global. The Columbian Exchange moved plants, animals, people, and diseases between the hemispheres; the Manila Galleon Trade (1565 to 1815) carried Chinese goods to the Americas and American silver to Asia, much of it from Potosi, where the Spanish organized labor through the mita; and the Dutch East India Company, chartered in 1602, was among the first companies to issue tradable shares and had powers to wage war and build forts.
  • Coerced labor underpinned much of the Atlantic economy. The Atlantic Slave Trade forcibly transported about 12.5 million Africans to the Americas, the Sugar Plantation Complex drove much of the demand, the Haitian Revolution arose in Saint-Domingue, the largest sugar producer in the world in the late 18th century, and the Abolition of Slavery followed between 1807 and 1888.
  • The Industrial Revolution began in Britain about 1760 with the shift to machine production driven by coal and steam, and economic output per person began to rise steadily for the first time in history. The Steam Engine, Railways, the Telegraph and Submarine Cables, the Electrical Power Grid, and the Suez Canal, which cut the voyage between Europe and India by thousands of kilometers, reshaped trade in the 19th century.
  • Modern economies were shaped by empire and by state policy. The Opium Wars opened China to Western commerce on unequal terms, the Scramble for Africa and the Congo Free State built forced-labor extraction, and after 1950 the Great Acceleration raised output and energy use steeply. Chinese Reform and Opening (from December 1978) brought market reforms and decades of rapid growth, the Digital Revolution spread computing and networks, and the COVID-19 Pandemic disrupted supply chains worldwide.

extra.title: Through the Eras
extra.html:
• Paleolithic: Stone, shell, and pigment moved between hunter-gatherer groups over long distances, but the evidence is fragmentary and the vault has no dedicated note on Paleolithic exchange; see Paleolithic.
  • Neolithic: Farming and herding (The Agricultural Revolution, Animal Domestication) created storable surpluses and traction animals, and Pottery allowed food and liquids to be stored and transported.
  • Bronze Age: The Urban Revolution, Uruk, Sumerians, Invention of Writing, Bronze Metallurgy, The Wheel, the Indus Valley Civilization, the Minoans, the Hittites, Hatshepsut's expedition to Punt, Caral, Poverty Point, the Lapita Culture, and the Bronze Age Collapse.
  • Iron Age: The Incense Trade, the Kingdom of Saba, the Phoenicians, Carthage, the Scythians, Samarkand, the Olmecs, the Achaemenid Persians, and Iron Smelting.
  • Classical Antiquity: The Opening of the Silk Roads, the Han Dynasty and Xiongnu, the Romans and Augustus, the Nabataeans, the Kushan Empire, the Sogdians, the Kingdom of Aksum, Teotihuacan, the Maurya Empire, and Zero and Place-Value Notation, which made calculation easier.
  • Medieval Period: The Indian Ocean Trade Network, the Swahili Coast City-States, Srivijaya, the Abbasid Caliphate, the Tang Dynasty and Song Dynasty, the Ghana Empire, Mali Empire, and Timbuktu, Great Zimbabwe, the Kingdom of Mapungubwe, Chaco Canyon, Cahokia, the Mongol Empire, whose relay postal system sped communication across Eurasia, the Norse, who traded in eastern Europe for silver from the Islamic world, the Malacca Sultanate, Zheng He, Ibn Battuta, and the Black Death.
  • Early Modern Period: The Columbian Exchange, the Portuguese Sea Route to India, the Manila Galleon Trade, Potosi, the Dutch East India Company, the Atlantic Slave Trade, the Sugar Plantation Complex, the Ming Dynasty, the Mughal Empire, which by 1700 ruled about 100 million people and made India one of the world's largest economies, the Tokugawa Shogunate, and the Russian Expansion into Siberia, driven by the fur trade.
  • Industrial Age: The Industrial Revolution, Railways, the Telegraph and Submarine Cables, the Electrical Power Grid, the Suez Canal, the Trans-Siberian Railway, the Opium Wars, the British Raj, the Scramble for Africa, the Congo Free State, the Abolition of Slavery, and the Bengal Famine of 1943, which Amartya Sen analyzed as an entitlement failure: food supply did not fall sharply, but economic pressures kept some groups from buying it.
  • Information Age: Decolonization, the Green Revolution, the Great Acceleration, the Digital Revolution, Chinese Reform and Opening, and the COVID-19 Pandemic.

extra.title: Regional Patterns
extra.html:
• Sub-Saharan Africa: Gold, salt, and ivory sustained the Sahelian empires and Swahili city-states, and the interior states of Mapungubwe and Great Zimbabwe reached the Indian Ocean; from the 16th century the Kingdom of Kongo was drawn into the Atlantic slave trade (Atlantic Slave Trade), and between 1885 and 1908 the Congo Free State extracted rubber and ivory by forced labor.
  • Central Asian Oases and the Central Asian Steppe: The Sogdians of the oases were the leading Silk Road merchants, and steppe powers such as the Xiongnu and the Mongol Empire taxed, protected, and raided the routes; see Samarkand.
  • Southeast Asia: Control of the straits made Srivijaya and the Malacca Sultanate rich, Champa traded across the South China Sea, and later the Manila Galleon Trade and the Dutch East India Company (which founded Batavia in 1619) tied the region to European and American markets.
  • Andes: Caral linked coast and highland, the Inca Empire ran a state economy on labor service and recorded goods on Quipu, and after the Spanish conquest the silver of Potosi, worked under a forced-labor draft adapted from an Inca system, supplied world trade.
  • Mesoamerica: Domestication of Maize made a staple crop for the Americas, Teotihuacan had wide trade links, and the Aztec Empire collected tribute from conquered city-states for Tenochtitlan.
  • Oceania: The Lapita Culture and later the Polynesians moved goods and people across thousands of kilometers of sea, and the Treaty of Waitangi of 1840 was followed by conflict over land and authority.
  • Siberia and the Arctic: European demand for furs drove the Russian Expansion into Siberia between 1582 and 1639, and the Yakut (Sakha) paid yasak, a fur tribute, until 1917; the Trans-Siberian Railway later linked the region to markets. See Frontiers of Extraction.
  • East Asia: The Tang and Song economies, the Ming reliance on American silver, Tokugawa restriction of foreign trade, the Opium Wars, and Chinese Reform and Opening mark shifts between openness and control.

extra.title: Debates and Limits
extra.html:
• The origins of markets and money are disputed. Whether exchange began as gift-giving, barter, credit, or tribute is argued, and the earliest written records, such as the tablets of Uruk, show accounting for obligations rather than simple barter.
  • The size and reach of early exchange are inferred from scattered goods, and estimates change. The extent and end of the Ghana Empire are debated, and older population estimates for Great Zimbabwe of 10,000 to 20,000 have been revised down to no more than about 10,000.
  • What counts as trade is contested, because exchange, tribute, and coercion overlap. The mita at Potosi, yasak in Siberia, forced rubber collection in the Congo Free State, and the Atlantic Slave Trade are extraction, and scholars disagree about how much slave-based commerce contributed to industrialization.
  • Why Britain and Europe industrialized first, and why sustained growth began when it did, is debated, and the Industrial Revolution note does not settle the causes.
  • The vault's coverage is uneven. It has one note on a company (Dutch East India Company) and none yet on coinage, paper money, credit, or double-entry bookkeeping as institutions, and it has few notes on the internal economies of Africa, Oceania, and the Americas.

theme/war-and-conflict.title: War and Conflict
theme/war-and-conflict.summary: War and conflict are organized violence between groups: raids, battles and sieges, conquests, rebellions, civil wars, and genocides, together with the treaties and settlements that end them. The vault follows them from the uneven evidence for violence in prehistory, through the chariot armies and iron-armed empires of antiquity, the steppe conquests and gunpowder states of the medieval and early modern worlds, and the colonial and revolutionary wars of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, to the industrial world wars and the nuclear standoff of the twentieth. The scale and character of organized violence has changed with technology, political organization, and the ability to feed, move, and command large forces. This hub records atrocity plainly as atrocity and notes where casualty figures and causes are disputed.
theme/war-and-conflict.observer: The Observer calls this sanctioned harm: violence that a group approves through its story-glue. It notes how the same species that holds strong inhibitions against killing individuals can, under the right story-glue, organize mass killing, and it records the harm plainly as harm. It notes with equal seriousness the counter-tradition of treaties, laws of war, and nonviolent movements, which appears as early as the treaty after the Battle of Kadesh and the edicts of Ashoka, and which states themselves often write. See Sanctioned Harm. This reading would weaken if organized killing proves to be explained mainly by scarcity or fear, with little role for shared stories that make it permissible.
questions: What conditions make large-scale organized violence more or less likely?
When did organized fighting between groups become common, and did settled life or the rise of states change its scale?
How did new technologies, such as the horse and chariot, iron, gunpowder, railways, and nuclear weapons, change who could wage war and how much of a society's effort it took?
Why do some wars end in durable settlements, such as the treaty after the Battle of Kadesh or the Peace of Westphalia, while others lead to renewed conflict?
How much of the death toll of war comes from famine and disease rather than combat, as in the Thirty Years' War and the Taiping Rebellion?
How do societies remember wars, and who controls the record?

extra.title: Key Threads
extra.html:
• Evidence for organized violence is uneven in early prehistory and grows with settled societies. The wall and tower at Jericho (about 8000 BCE) may have served defense or protection from floods, and the early city of Caral shows no evidence of large-scale warfare.
  • Bronze Age states fielded chariots and fortified centers. The Wheel and Bronze Metallurgy supplied vehicles and weapons, the Sintashta Culture built fortified settlements and the earliest known spoke-wheeled chariots, and at the Battle of Kadesh (about 1274 BCE) Egyptian and Hittites armies fought one of the largest chariot battles on record. About fifteen years later they concluded a peace treaty, of which versions survive in both archives. Around 1200 BCE many of these states collapsed within a few decades (Bronze Age Collapse; see also the Mycenaean Greeks).
  • Iron Age empires built large armies and administrations. Iron Smelting made it easier to arm large populations, the Neo-Assyrian Empire used mass deportation and controlled Mesopotamia, the Levant, and briefly Egypt, and the Achaemenid Persians under Cyrus the Great took Babylon in 539 BCE and built Persepolis. Alexander's Conquests (336 to 323 BCE) ended the Achaemenid Empire.
  • Rome and Carthage fought three Punic Wars between 264 and 146 BCE, and Rome destroyed Carthage in 146 BCE. Augustus ended a century of civil war and began the Pax Romana; the Fall of the Western Roman Empire in 476 CE was a long process that historians debate as either collapse or transformation. See Romans.
  • In East and South Asia, the Unification of China under Qin in 221 BCE under Qin Shi Huang created the first unified Chinese empire. The Han Dynasty faced the Xiongnu confederation, at times paying it in gifts and marriage alliances, and Ashoka of the Maurya Empire conquered Kalinga around 261 BCE, an event his own edicts record as killing about 100,000 people and deporting 150,000, after which he supported Buddhism and promoted moral conduct.
  • Steppe powers repeatedly confronted settled states. The Scythians were horse-riding nomads of the Iron Age, the Göktürk Khaganate ruled Inner Asia from about 552 CE, and from 1206 the Mongol Conquests under Genghis Khan built the largest contiguous land empire in history, including the sack of Baghdad in 1258; estimates of the deaths run to tens of millions and are uncertain. Timur later campaigned from Persia to India, sacking Delhi in 1398 and defeating the Ottoman sultan at Ankara in 1402.
  • Faith, empire, and firepower drove long wars. The Rise of Islam and the Umayyad Caliphate extended Muslim rule from Iberia to Sindh, the Battle of Talas in 751 ended Tang expansion in Central Asia, the Crusades began in 1095, and Gunpowder, developed in China and used by the Song in fire arrows, bombs, and early firearms, reached Europe by the 13th century. The Ottomans used very large cannon in the Fall of Constantinople in 1453.
  • Conquest and resistance shaped the early modern world. The Spanish Conquest of the Aztec Empire (1519 to 1521) relied on Indigenous allies and on smallpox, and the Spanish Conquest of the Inca Empire began in 1532 after an Inca civil war. The Mapuche resisted the Inca and then the Spanish for centuries, and Nzinga of Ndongo and Matamba used diplomacy and war against Portuguese expansion.
  • European wars built and tested states. The Thirty Years' War (1618 to 1648) killed up to about eight million people, mostly from famine and disease, and ended with the Peace of Westphalia; the Seven Years' War (1756 to 1763) was fought on several continents; and the Napoleonic Wars (1803 to 1815) ended at Waterloo and helped set off Latin American independence movements.
  • Revolutions and wars of independence recast who held power. See the Age of Revolutions, the American Revolution, the French Revolution, the Haitian Revolution, and the Latin American Wars of Independence, and, later, the Mexican Revolution, the Russian Revolution, and the Xinhai Revolution.
  • Wars between the Qing state, Britain, and rebels shook Asia in the 19th century: the Opium Wars opened China to Western commerce on unequal terms, the Taiping Rebellion (1850 to 1864) killed an estimated 20 to 30 million people, and the Indian Rebellion of 1857 ended East India Company rule (British Raj).
  • Wars of conquest and defense reshaped Africa and the settler colonies. The Zulu Kingdom under Shaka became a large military state and the Mfecane followed; the Scramble for Africa raised the share of the continent under European control from roughly 10 percent to about 90 percent between 1881 and 1914; Ethiopia won the Battle of Adwa in 1896; and Indian Removal and the Trail of Tears and the First Fleet and the Colonization of Australia led to dispossession and death for Native American and Aboriginal peoples.
  • Industrial war reached unprecedented scale. Railways, telegraphs, and factories shaped the American Civil War; World War I killed roughly 10 million soldiers and brought down four empires; World War II killed an estimated 60 to 85 million people, including about six million Jews murdered in the Holocaust. The Armenian Genocide and the Second Sino-Japanese War, including the killings at Nanjing, show mass killing of civilians.
  • Nuclear Fission, discovered in 1938, made nuclear weapons possible, and the Nuclear Age began with the first test in July 1945. The Cold War (about 1947 to 1991) was fought through arms races, alliances, and proxy wars, and ended with the Collapse of the Soviet Union; Decolonization was won by negotiation and by war, and the Partition of India in 1947 brought mass migration and violence.

extra.title: Through the Eras
extra.html:
• Paleolithic: Clear evidence for organized fighting between groups is scarce, and scholars disagree about how common it was. DNA shows interbreeding among Homo sapiens, Homo neanderthalensis, and Denisovans, so contact between human groups was not only conflict. See Paleolithic.
  • Neolithic: Settled life brought walls, stored food, and land to defend (The Agricultural Revolution, Jericho), though the purpose of the early wall at Jericho is debated.
  • Bronze Age: Unification of Egypt around 3100 BCE, the king of Babylon Hammurabi, the Sintashta Culture and its chariots, the Hittites and Egypt at the Battle of Kadesh, the Mycenaean Greeks, the Shang Dynasty, and the Bronze Age Collapse.
  • Iron Age: Iron Smelting, the Neo-Assyrian Empire, the Scythians, the Kingdom of Kush, which ruled Egypt as its 25th Dynasty, the Achaemenid Persians under Cyrus the Great, and Carthage.
  • Classical Antiquity: Alexander the Great and Alexander's Conquests, Rome and the Romans under Augustus, the Unification of China under Qin, the Han Dynasty and the Xiongnu, the Maurya Empire and Ashoka, the Byzantine Empire, and the Fall of the Western Roman Empire.
  • Medieval Period: The Rise of Islam, the Umayyad Caliphate, the Battle of Talas, Norse raids from 793, the Crusades, the Mongol Conquests, Timur, the Fall of Constantinople, and Gunpowder; the Classic Maya Collapse, in which warfare is among the proposed causes; and the Chola Dynasty, whose fleet struck Srivijaya around 1025.
  • Early Modern Period: The Spanish Conquest of the Aztec Empire and Spanish Conquest of the Inca Empire, the Thirty Years' War, the Peace of Westphalia, the Seven Years' War, the Russian Expansion into Siberia, the Dutch East India Company, the Mapuche, and Nzinga of Ndongo and Matamba. Japan under the Tokugawa Shogunate enjoyed a long period of peace from 1603 to 1868.
  • Industrial Age: The Napoleonic Wars, Haitian Revolution, Latin American Wars of Independence, Opium Wars, Taiping Rebellion, American Civil War, Scramble for Africa, Battle of Adwa, World War I, Armenian Genocide, Turkish War of Independence, Second Sino-Japanese War, World War II, and the Holocaust.
  • Information Age: The Nuclear Age, the Cold War, Decolonization, the Partition of India, and the Collapse of the Soviet Union.

extra.title: Regional Patterns
extra.html:
• Mesopotamia, the Levant and Anatolia, and the Nile Valley: The great powers of the Bronze Age and Iron Age, Egypt, the Hittites, and Assyria, fought over the Levant and left battle and treaty records on more than one side; see the Battle of Kadesh and the Neo-Assyrian Empire.
  • Central Asian Steppe: Mobile pastoral powers (Scythians, Xiongnu, Göktürk Khaganate, Mongol Empire) repeatedly confronted settled states, from the Han frontier to Baghdad and Eastern Europe.
  • East Asia: Unification under Qin, the Han wars with the Xiongnu, Song use of gunpowder weapons, Ming construction of much of the Great Wall in its present form, and the Qing expansion to its greatest extent were followed by the Opium Wars, Taiping Rebellion, Boxer Rebellion, and Second Sino-Japanese War; see Song Dynasty, Ming Dynasty, and Qing Dynasty.
  • Sub-Saharan Africa: Wars of state-building (Zulu Kingdom, Sokoto Caliphate) and of resistance (Kingdom of Kongo, Nzinga of Ndongo and Matamba, Battle of Adwa, the British conquest of Kingdom of Benin in 1897) were followed by the forced labor and mass deaths of the Congo Free State (1885 to 1908).
  • Mesoamerica and the Andes: The Aztec Empire collected tribute from conquered city-states, whose resentment helped the Spanish; the Inca Empire expanded under Pachacuti; and warfare is among the proposed causes of the Classic Maya Collapse, for which no single cause is accepted.
  • Southeast Asia: Champa was gradually conquered by Vietnam until its last remnant was annexed in 1832, the Pagan Kingdom fell to Mongol armies in 1287, Ayutthaya Kingdom was destroyed by Burmese forces in 1767, and the Dutch East India Company used force to secure monopolies.
  • Oceania: The First Fleet and the Colonization of Australia began conflict and dispossession for Aboriginal Australians, and disputes over land and authority after the Treaty of Waitangi led to the New Zealand Wars of the 1840s to 1870s.
  • Siberia and the Arctic: Russian Cossacks and traders advanced to the Pacific between 1582 and 1639 for furs and tribute (Russian Expansion into Siberia), and the Yakut (Sakha) revolted against Russian rule in 1642.

extra.title: Debates and Limits
extra.html:
• Scholars disagree about how common organized warfare was in prehistory, and about whether it grew mainly with settled societies and states. The evidence is mostly skeletal injury, fortification, and weapons, and it can be read in more than one way.
  • Casualty figures are uncertain and sometimes politically contested: the deaths from the Mongol Conquests (tens of millions, uncertain), the Congo Free State (about 1 million to 15 million), the Taiping Rebellion (20 to 30 million), the killings at Nanjing in the Second Sino-Japanese War, and the Armenian Genocide, which the Turkish state denies.
  • Causes are often disputed. Historians debate whether the Fall of the Western Roman Empire was a collapse or a transformation, and many regard the common claim that the Peace of Westphalia created the sovereign-state system as a later simplification. They also disagree about the scale and causes of the Mfecane and the role of Shaka. The Bronze Age Collapse and the Classic Maya Collapse have no single accepted cause.
  • Many accounts come from the winners or from hostile writers: the accounts of Shaka come largely from colonial-era Europeans and oral tradition, later chronicles describe massacres by Timur with contested numbers, and later historians hostile to the Qin described harsh punishments that are debated.
  • The vault covers a selection of conflicts. It has notes on only three individual battles (Battle of Kadesh, Battle of Talas, Battle of Adwa) and none yet on naval, air, or guerrilla warfare as topics, on the Korean War or the Vietnam War beyond their mention under the Cold War, or on conflicts after 1991.
